characters.name: George Milton
characters.tagline: Small, quick, protective — the father figure

branches.title: Appearance
extra: "Every part of him was defined: small, strong hands, slender arms, a thin and bony nose" — a sharp body for a sharp mind

branches.title: Father figure
nodes: Cares for Lennie even if it doesn't benefit him
Like a father figure to Lennie
"Think I'd let you carry your own work card" — father-like figure, understands Lennie [p.8]
Knew he would put Lennie in danger, but didn't care (Sacramento River)
extra: Does the talking in front of the boss, hiding Lennie's disability so they both get the job
Tells Slim he once told Lennie to jump in the river and he nearly drowned — he stopped playing tricks on him after that

branches.title: Temper
nodes: Short temper: "George exploded" → "working up a slow anger"
Says to Lennie: "you'd drink out of a gutter if you was thirsty"
"I hate his guts" — talking about Curley
"I could get along so easy if I didn't have you" [p.8]
extra: His anger never lasts — he softens and tells Lennie about the rabbits, so it reads as frustration, not cruelty

branches.title: The dream
extra: "Guys like us, that work on ranches, are the loneliest guys in the world" — but they have each other
Tells the dream like a bedtime story — Lennie knows it by heart and joins in
"I think I knowed from the very first. I think I knowed we'd never do her" — the dream dies with Lennie

branches.title: Ending & journey
extra: Shoots Lennie by the pool where the novel began — a mercy killing, so Lennie dies happy and not at Curley's hands
Mirrors Candy, who said he should have shot his own dog — George won't let a stranger do it
Ends up alone — one of the lonely ranch workers he described in Chapter 1

branches.title: Context
extra: ★ Itinerant (migrant) workers travelled alone from ranch to ranch — a pair like George and Lennie was unusual
★ The Great Depression (1929–39): jobs were scarce and short, with no welfare if you lost one
★ The American Dream: owning your own land through hard work — George's dream shows how out of reach it was

links: I could get along so easy
I think I knowed from the very first
Knew he would put Lennie in danger
Tells Slim he once told Lennie

characters.name: Lennie Small
characters.tagline: Huge, gentle, childlike — and dangerous without meaning to be

branches.title: Animal imagery
nodes: Walks like "a bear drags his paws"
Compared to animals due to not understanding things
To convey how Lennie is different
Animals are also innocent — so is Lennie

branches.title: Childlike
nodes: Appears to have a low IQ / mentally impaired intellectual ability
"He's a nice fella" · "He's jes' like a kid" — Slim
extra: "I remember about the rabbits, George" — forgets almost everything except the dream
"If you don' want me I can go off in the hills an' find a cave" — a child threatening to run away

branches.title: Strength & danger
nodes: Does not understand the consequences of his actions
Obsession with soft things → foreshadows idea of danger / problematic obsession
Gentle giant — some of the time
extra: Kills mice, then his puppy, then Curley's wife — each death bigger, building to the climax
"Curley was flopping like a fish on a line" — crushes Curley's hand without meaning harm
In Weed he grabbed a girl's red dress because it was soft and wouldn't let go — Curley's wife is the same story again

branches.title: Sympathy
nodes: Lennie's eyes were "frightened" — Steinbeck tries to make us sympathise with him
As much a victim as his victims
extra: "You ain't so little as mice" — confused and sad over the dead puppy, not cruel

branches.title: The dream
extra: "An' live off the fatta the lan'" — he finishes George's sentences: the farm is his favourite story
"I got you to look after me, and you got me to look after you" — why they're different from other workers
Dies looking across the river while George describes the farm — happy at the very end

branches.title: Context
extra: ★ People with learning disabilities were often locked in institutions in the 1930s — Lennie has no protection except George
★ Steinbeck said Lennie was based on a real man he worked alongside on a ranch

links: I got you to look after me
You ain't so little as mice
Appears to have a low IQ

characters.name: Candy
characters.tagline: The old swamper who fears being thrown away

branches.title: His old dog
nodes: His dog is: "G-d damn old" · "stinks like hell"
Had the dog "since he was a pup"
When his dog was shot, he "turned to the wall"
extra: "I ought to of shot that dog myself, George. I shouldn't ought to of let no stranger shoot my dog"
Carlson shoots the dog because it is old and useless — the ranch has no room for anything weak

branches.title: Age & disability
nodes: Disabled physically → missing right hand ("stick-like wrist")
Product of the harsh ranch world
extra: "When they can me here I wisht somebody'd shoot me" — he fears ending up like his dog

branches.title: Gossip & prejudice
nodes: A gossip — gossips to make conversation: lonely himself · is vulnerable · looks to establish connections
Uses "tart" to describe Curley's wife — a derogatory term that draws prejudice towards her before we meet her [p.9]
extra: Insults Curley's wife even over her dead body — blames her for ruining the dream

branches.title: The dream
extra: "S'pose I went in with you guys. Tha's three hundred an' fifty bucks I'd put in" — his savings make the dream real
The farm would give him a home and a purpose in old age, instead of being thrown away
After Curley's wife dies he begs George to still buy the farm with him — George can't

branches.title: Context
extra: ★ The Social Security Act (1935) was brand new and left out farm workers — no pension for men like Candy
★ He got $250 for losing his hand — injured workers had almost no protection

links: The farm would give him a home

characters.name: Crooks
characters.tagline: The stable buck — isolated by racism

branches.title: Racism & isolation
nodes: Described as the "n-word" before his personality
extra: "I ain't wanted in the bunk house, and you ain't wanted in my room"
Lives alone in the harness room by the barn — kept apart from the white men
"They play cards in there, but I can't play because I'm black"

branches.title: Body & work
nodes: Kicked by a horse → crooked back (why he's called Crooks)
extra: "More permanent than the other men" — he owns more things, but he's trapped on the ranch

branches.title: Pride & status
extra: "Crooks was a proud, aloof man. He kept his distance and demanded that other people keep theirs"
Keeps a dictionary and a copy of the California civil code — he knows his rights but can't use them
Taunts Lennie that George might not come back — enjoys power over someone weaker for once

branches.title: Loneliness & the dream
extra: "A guy needs somebody—to be near him"
"Nobody never gets to heaven, and nobody gets no land" — he's seen the dream fail many times
Grew up on his father's chicken ranch in California — he once had what George and Lennie dream of
Asks to join the dream, then takes it back: "Jus' foolin'. I wouldn' want to go no place like that"

branches.title: Curley's wife's threat
extra: "I could get you strung up on a tree so easy it ain't even funny" — Curley's wife
"Crooks had reduced himself to nothing" — he has no power against a white woman

branches.title: Context
nodes: ★ The average black person in 1930s America was: discriminated against · dehumanised · marginalised
extra: ★ Lynching: a white woman's word could get a black man killed by a mob — her threat is real
★ Jim Crow laws segregated the South, and racism was normal across 1930s America

links: Crooks had reduced himself to nothing
I could get you strung up
Lives alone in the harness room
More permanent than the other men

characters.name: Curley
characters.tagline: The boss's son — small, insecure, looking for a fight

branches.title: Aggression
nodes: Sees the ranch as a battleground, not a workplace
"Next time you answer when you're spoken to"
extra: "His glance was at once calculating and pugnacious"

branches.title: Small & insecure
nodes: "Ants in his pants" — nervous and tense

branches.title: Power & status
nodes: Can behave how he likes as he's the boss's son
George calls him a "punk" — knows straight away he'll cause problems [p.21]
extra: Picks on Lennie because he's big and doesn't fight back — a bully choosing a safe target

branches.title: Marriage
nodes: Ignores wife; thinks love is physical, not emotional → "glove full of vaseline"
extra: Boasts about his marriage but never spends time with his wife — possessive, not loving

branches.title: Fight & revenge
extra: "Curley was flopping like a fish on a line" — Lennie crushes his hand
Agrees to say his hand got caught in a machine — too proud to admit he lost
"I'm gonna shoot the guts outa that big bastard myself, even if I only got one hand" — revenge, not grief

branches.title: Context
extra: ★ Ranch owners' families had total power — a worker who stood up to Curley could be fired on the spot
★ 1930s masculinity valued toughness and fighting — boxing is Curley's way of proving he's a man

characters.name: Curley's Wife
characters.tagline: The only woman on the ranch — and never given a name

branches.title: Appearance & danger
extra: "She had full, rouged lips and wide-spaced eyes, heavily made up. Her fingernails were red"
"The rectangle of sunshine in the doorway was cut off" — she literally blocks out the light

branches.title: No name, no power
nodes: We hear about her before we meet her — Steinbeck wants us to draw prejudice towards her (see p.31)

branches.title: Marriage
nodes: Looks for attention, which Curley doesn't give
Wants an emotional connection with Curley
Possessive / disharmony (possession of Curley) → contrast to the natural world
Curley's wife and Curley are not seen together [p.9]
extra: "I don' like Curley. He ain't a nice fella"

branches.title: Lonely & dreams
nodes: Seeks conversation with the ranch workers as she seeks conversation in a male-orientated society
extra: "Why can't I talk to you? I never get to talk to nobody. I get awful lonely"
"Coulda been in the movies, an' had nice clothes" — her lost Hollywood dream
Threatens Crooks with lynching — cruel to the one person with less power than her

branches.title: Death
extra: "The meanness and the plannings and the discontent and the ache for attention were all gone from her face" — Steinbeck finally lets us pity her

branches.title: Context
nodes: ★ Women gained the right to vote in 1920, but social attitudes remained largely patriarchal [p.24]
extra: ★ 1930s women were expected to be wives and mothers, with few jobs or rights of their own
★ Hollywood was booming in the 1930s — films sold ordinary girls a dream of fame
★ Steinbeck wrote to the actress playing her (1938) that she was "not a floozy" — just lonely

links: Why can't I talk to you

characters.name: Slim

branches.title: Natural authority
nodes: Authority — "his word was taken on any subject"
Doesn't need to show his authority
"Slim don't need to wear high-heeled boots"
extra: "He moved with a majesty only achieved by royalty and master craftsmen"

branches.title: Appearance & skill
extra: So skilled with a bull whip he could kill a fly on a mule's rump without touching the mule

branches.title: Wisdom
nodes: Makes George tell Slim things — there was "calm"
extra: "I can tell a mean guy from a mile off" — sees straight away that Lennie isn't dangerous
"Maybe ever'body in the whole damn world is scared of each other" — wonders why so few men travel together

branches.title: Compassion
extra: Drowns four of his dog's new puppies but gives one to Lennie — kind, but practical
Backs Carlson over Candy's dog: "I wisht somebody'd shoot me if I got old an' a cripple"
"You hadda, George. I swear you hadda" — the only one who understands why George shot Lennie

branches.title: Context
extra: ★ A jerkline skinner drove a big mule team with a single line — the most skilled, respected job on a ranch
★ Slim can be read as Steinbeck's ideal working man — respect that comes from skill, not money

links: Drowns four of his dog's new puppies

characters.name: The Boss
characters.tagline: Owns the land — and everyone's job

branches.title: Power & status
extra: Never given a name — defined only by his power, just as Curley's wife is defined by her husband

branches.title: Appearance
nodes: Both the boss and his son Curley wear high-heeled boots — shows authority, wealth and status [p.9]
extra: "He wore high-heeled boots and spurs to prove he was not a laboring man"

branches.title: Suspicion
nodes: "Looked for a long moment at the 2 men"
"What stake you got in this guy?" [p.18]
extra: "Well, I never seen one guy take so much trouble for another guy" — friendship looks suspicious on the ranch
Suspects George is taking Lennie's pay — he can't imagine a friendship without a catch

branches.title: Business first
extra: Angry that the men arrived late — he cares about the lost work, not the workers
Candy says he once brought the men a gallon of whisky at Christmas — not cruel, just distant
Appears only once — the owner's power works from a distance

branches.title: Context
extra: ★ A few big landowners controlled California farming — workers owned nothing and could be sacked at any time
★ He represents the class system: the owner already has the land the workers can only dream of

settings.name: The Natural World
settings.tagline: The Salinas River pool — calm, green, Eden-like

branches.title: Peace & beauty
nodes: "Hillside bank and runs deep and green"
Peaceful and harmonious with the repetition of green → hope, possibility
"Gentle movement of animals" → contributes to the calm atmosphere

branches.title: Eden
extra: A safe place — George tells Lennie to come back and hide in the brush here if he gets into trouble

branches.title: Contrast & structure
nodes: Clear juxtaposition between the calm natural world and the money-minded farm
extra: The novel begins and ends at this pool — a cyclical structure: George and Lennie end up where they started

branches.title: Chapter 6: Eden spoiled
extra: "A silent head and beak lanced down and plucked it out by the head" — the heron kills the water snake, foreshadowing Lennie's death
Nature is beautiful but also cruel — the weak are killed by the strong, just like on the ranch

branches.title: Context
extra: ★ Steinbeck grew up in Salinas, California, and knew this valley and river well

links: Nature is beautiful but also cruel

settings.name: The Bunkhouse
settings.tagline: Where the men live — bare, stark, functional

branches.title: Stark & bare
extra: "Over each bunk there was nailed an apple box" — a man's whole life fits on two shelves

branches.title: Contrast
extra: No privacy and no comfort — the men are treated as tools for work, like the building itself

branches.title: Life inside
extra: The men sit in silence in the bunkhouse waiting for the shot that kills Candy's dog
Cards, magazines and talk of town fill the evenings — a lonely, temporary life

branches.title: Context
extra: ★ Bunkhouses housed migrant workers for a season at a time — nobody stayed long enough to belong

incidents.title: The Bus Driver
incidents.what: The bus drops George and Lennie off miles short of the ranch, so they have to walk the rest.
notes: Bus driver incident — "crazy bastard" — shows George's short temper [p.8]

incidents.title: The Ketchup Incident
incidents.what: As they eat beans by the fire, Lennie says he likes them with ketchup.
notes: "George exploded" because Lennie asked for ketchup [p.8]
Ketchup incident shows Lennie's bad memory and George's short temper [p.8]
Short temper: "George exploded" → "working up a slow anger" [p.12]

incidents.title: The Dead Mouse
incidents.what: Lennie has been carrying a dead mouse in his pocket to pet it; George makes him hand it over and throws it away.
notes: "They was dead, because they was so little" → tragic disconnect between intent and consequences [p.8]
Obsession with soft things → foreshadows idea of danger / problematic obsession [p.11]
incidents.para_title: How does Steinbeck use the incident of the mouse?
incidents.para: Lennie's obsession with petting soft things (mice, puppies and eventually Curley's wife's hair) is used by Steinbeck to highlight his childlike innocence, but it is, as we will see, this habit that leads to accidental violence, with him confessing that with the animals he pinched their heads then "they was dead, because they was so little." This highlights a tragic disconnect between intention and consequence; like an animal that doesn't know its own strength, Lennie kills it without meaning to. He treats mice and dogs like toys, but his lack of control, both physical and mental, turns these reactions deadly.

incidents.title: The Sacramento River
incidents.what: George admits that he once told Lennie to jump into the Sacramento River, even though Lennie couldn't swim.
notes: Knew that he would put Lennie in danger, but didn't care [p.12]
incidents.para: In Chapter 3, George has a conversation with Slim and confesses that he "used to play jokes" on Lennie and that he had once made Lennie [jump] into the Sacramento River, even with the fact George knew Lennie couldn't swim. Steinbeck uses this to show George's early immaturity and shows Lennie follows all orders from George like a father and son would. Over time George stops using his power on Lennie as he realises, after Lennie's near-death experience, that he has a duty to look after Lennie, so won't treat him that way again.

incidents.title: The Shooting of Candy's Dog
incidents.what: Carlson pressures Candy into letting him take the old dog outside and shoot it.
notes: When the dog was shot, Candy "turned to the wall" [p.16]
Had the dog "since he was a pup" [p.16]
incidents.para: In Chapter 3 of Of Mice and Men, Steinbeck's portrayal of Carlson's unceremonious shooting of Candy's dog is used to highlight the brutal pragmatism of ranch life and the dehumanising effects of the Great Depression and the hardships it produced. The dog is described as "old"; language which reduces it to a burden rather than a companion, reflecting a society that values usefulness over emotional connection. Carlson's insistence that the dog should be shot emphasises the cold, utilitarian mindset. Carlson lists all the things the dog "can't" do, but fails to see what it can do. The lack of ceremony in the killing, being done "offstage" as it were, with the "shot" breaking the bunkhouse silence. Candy's acquiescence reveals his awareness that he, too, is ageing, foreshadowing the fear of being cast aside when he is no longer of use.

paragraphs.title: How Steinbeck Introduces Curley
paragraphs.text: Steinbeck introduces Curley as an aggressive, insecure figure who relies on a strong posture to convey his apparent strength and dominance. Upon meeting the two men, Curley immediately shifts into a fighting stance, with his "hands closed into fists." This tense and angry reaction shows his hostility towards the men due to the fact he feels threatened by the larger men. It is interesting to note "his high-heeled boots" which signifies a desire to elevate his posture and the desire to stop being a "small guy" and to show off his authority. As well as this, when George meets the "pugnacious" Curley for the first time, George refers to Curley as a "punk", suggesting that he knows straight away that he is going to cause problems.

paragraphs.title: How Steinbeck Introduces Curley's Wife
paragraphs.text: Steinbeck introduces Curley's wife as an isolated person. When she is first in the bunkhouse, she stands in the "doorway", which portrays her as a threat to the men as she is standing over them. She is wearing "red," which is a clear contrast to the brown "whitewashed" bunkhouse. This shows her clear difference to the men and emphasises that people with authority (Curley, his wife and the boss) wear clothes to show their power. It is also interesting to note that Curley's wife is only referred to as "Curley's wife"; her name is not known. This and also the apostrophe on "Curley's" conveys the fact (due to the context of 1930s America) that Curley is the possessor of his wife and how she can be viewed as an object who can be owned.

feedback.target: When a word starts with a vowel, remember to use "an" — e.g. an isolated person, an apple, a chicken.

paragraphs.title: How Steinbeck Presents the Boss
paragraphs.text: The boss owns the land and controls the workers' jobs. This power makes him intimidating to the men and Steinbeck describes his flamboyant clothes to show his authority, such as the "square steel buckle" on his belt. Due to owning the land, the boss doesn't have to do "labor" or do manual work, which is suggested by his "high-heeled boots and spurs"; owning land gives him power to choose what he does and is a clear indication of why George and Lennie fixate upon owning "a little piece of land" themselves. Interestingly, we see the Boss is suspicious of George. We hear him ask "Say, what you selling?" and "What stake you got in this guy?" Steinbeck uses the Boss here to present a world where kindness and loyalty are unusual, causing people to distrust the friendship. The word "selling" implies deceit, as though George is trying to gain something from Lennie rather than simply helping him.

paragraphs.title: Embedding: George's "Own Crops"
paragraphs.text: We hear George, when confessing to Slim, suggest that "if I was bright" he would have his "own crops" instead of working for someone in a higher echelon. George implies that people at the bottom do the work but don't get the fruits of their labour. This highlights the injustice of a system which is exploitative.
